newsitem.title: CANADA: U.N. envoy sees Zaire mission longer than 6 months.
newsitem.headline: U.N. envoy sees Zaire mission longer than 6 months.

text.p: The United Nations envoy on the Zaire refugee crisis said on Wednesday he expected troops to have to stay in the area for longer than the initial six months currently being discussed.
"Initially, I think we're thinking of a mandate of six months," Ambassador Raymond Chretien said in an interview from Africa with the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
Pressed on whether all the troops would then head home, he said: "I don't think so...You know the history of those operations -- they tend to be extended if necessary."

Chretien, Canadian ambassador to Washington and nephew of Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien, said however that there was a tremendous political will in North America, Europe and Africa to deal with the issue and participate in the force.
Canadian Defence Minister Doug Young, however, spoke on Wednesday of a shorter period.
"We are looking at humanitarian aid for a period of six months or less," Young told reporters in the Quebec military base of Valcartier after a speech to troops.
One of the conditions in the U.S. agreement in principle to join the mission, announced by the White House on Wednesday, was that it be of limited duration.
Young said there had been no "final determination of the mandate" for the mission, which Canada has offered to head and to which it will contribute 1,500 of its own troops.
He added that he wanted "robust rules of engagement" for the international forces that will bring humanitarian aid to the hundreds of thousands of refugees caught up in the conflict in Zaire.
Ambassador Chretien said troops could be on the ground very quickly once the U.N. Security Council authorises the mission.

"In my view if the Security Council now moves fast -- and I think it will move fast following the American announcement in Washington -- it's a matter of 48 to 72 hours before the first contingent will show up in the region," he said.
As for Canada's troops, Young said they would be ready to mobilise within 48 to 72 hours of a Security Council decision.
Young also hinted he would prefer that Lt. Gen. Maurice Baril, commander of Canada's land forces, head the Canadian contingent.
"I would be very confident if it were to be Lt. Gen. Baril," Young said.

Baril was formerly a peacekeeping adviser to U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali. He has also been touted as a likely successor to Gen. Jean Boyle, who resigned last month as head of Canada's military forces over allegations of a coverup of the murder of Somalis in 1993 during Canadian peacekeeping operations in Somalia.
